newsitem.title: USA: Purchasers group sees higher growth, scant price pressure.
newsitem.headline: Purchasers group sees higher growth, scant price pressure.

text.p: The economy will slow temporarily from the first quarter's torrid pace of growth but should pick up steam again in the second half of the year, purchasing executives and a leading business economist said Tuesday.

The National Association of Purchasing Management said economic growth will be "somewhat higher" in the second half of the year, according to its 53rd survey of its members, who buy raw and processed materials for about 300 major manufacturers.
"Purchasing executives report a higher level of optimism for the coming year than they did a year ago," said Norbert Ore, chairman of the group's business survey committee.
Meanwhile, Conference Board Chief Economist Gail Fosler predicted strong economic growth of about 3.25 percent to 3.5 percent for all of 1997. The economy grew 2.4 percent last year.

Growth soared to a blistering 5.6 percent annual rate in the first quarter -- the strongest pace in more than nine years -- the government said last week, though most economists expect that to slow in the current quarter.
With economic growth strong, Fosler said corporate profits would rise at least 10 percent this year from higher prices and an increase in sales.

"There will be a decided effort to look for opportunities to raise prices," she said at the purchasing association's semiannual meeting. Fosler noted that companies' labour and energy costs are on the rise.

But she said there was no risk of a significant rise in inflation or a major economic downturn in the next two to three years and that she did not expect higher interest rates to be a threat to the economy, at least this year.
The Federal Reserve raised rates in March for the first time in more than two years in a bid to keep growth in check and ward off inflation.
Fosler said the central bank was likely to raise rates again when its policy-makers meet on May 20.

"Then, frankly I don't think they'll do very much until the second half of the year when the stubborness and durability of this economic environment really makes itself felt once again as it has early in the year," she said.
While the stock market is likely to be erratic in 1997, investors can expect continued high returns over a three- to four-year period, Fosler said.
"These are the best economic times in a generation," she said. "We're going to see very, very high rates of return."

Purchasing executives predicted manufacturing employment will increase in 1997, with 30 percent expecting to add workers, up from the 26 percent who predicted higher employment this year in the last survey in December.

The purchasing executives expressed little concern over possible increases in costs for raw materials. They said prices paid for materials -- widely watched as a gauge of inflation -- fell 0.2 percent in the first four months of 1997 and were expected to rise 0.7 percent for the full year.
Overall labour and benefit costs are expected to rise 2.4 percent, the survey said.
